Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
**This is a good briefing, and its structure is right.** It weighs evidence by design strength, keeps the per-hour and per-worker questions apart, separates discretionary from coverage-bound work, rejects both slogans, and leaves the right big questions open. It represents the five sources accurately.

Its main weakness is typical of syntheses: **caveats get lost as findings move up the chain of summaries.** The mediation result is the clearest example:
- **Source 2:** "suggests, cannot establish a mechanism."
- **Source 5:** "confirms."
- **Synthesis, point 4:** "about half the per-hour gain… comes from removing recurring meetings."
- **Bottom line:** "about half of it through fewer meetings," now applied to discretionary work in general.

Each step is a small rounding up, and together they turn a single-setting result into a general mechanism. Several other points follow the same pattern.

Some of what follows rests only on points I raised in earlier replies, not on anything in the five sources. I've marked those, because the briefing can't be faulted for missing them.

## Accuracy against the sources

The figures are transcribed correctly: 23.4, 12.5 and 6.7, the 22% scheduled-hours figure, 3.8 points, 14.1%, −2.6% real, 10.8, 13.4, 8.2, 7.9, 9.7, 9.6, 9.1, 8.5, −3.4, 47/18/35, and 11.8. There are two misstatements.

**1. The decline compares figures measured in different ways.** "Declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)" repeats source 5's own error:
- 12.5% is from timesheets; 8.5% is from system logs.
- On the same measure (timesheets), the change is **12.5% → 9.8%**.
- The two intervals overlap substantially, so the decline itself isn't statistically established.

This can be seen from source 5's Table 1 alone.

**2. "Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong."** Source 5 showed that the claim was *unsupported*: the four long-follow-up studies couldn't test it. Source 5 also found one controlled study with a decline that isn't statistically clear. That doesn't make the claim false. "Unsupported" is the accurate word, and using "wrong" makes the same overreach the briefing rightly criticises in source 3.

## Problems in the weighing

**3. Table 1 doesn't show what the text claims.** The table is said to be "ordered by strength of design," and the text says estimates "fall as designs strengthen." The order isn't consistent with that, and the values don't fall steadily: 23.4, 11.8, 10.8, 13.4, 9.1, 9.6, **12.5**, 8.5, 6.7.
- The randomised nine-month estimate (12.5%) is higher than the uncontrolled corrected one (10.8%).
- The last row is counter work, a different type of work. Putting it at the bottom makes the trend look steeper than it is.

The table does support a narrower conclusion: **the features that move the estimate are the hours measure and the output measure**, and estimates computed on actual hours cluster around 8–12%. The table should separate discretionary from coverage-bound estimates and drop the claim of a steady fall.

**4. The "convergence" isn't independent.**
- Source 4's subgroups overlap with each other and with sources 1 and 2, both of which it includes.
- Source 5's Varden estimate covers the same offices as source 2.

The 8–10% range is real, but it rests on fewer independent studies than the list of figures suggests.

**5. Point 2's arithmetic doesn't support its range.** It takes actual hours falling 11–14% and per-hour gains of 8–10%. Multiplying those gives per-worker output **2–7% lower**, not "2 to 4%."
- The 2–4% range matches the observed point estimates (Varden −2.1 and −3.4; meta-analysis −2.7).
- The briefing should cite those directly rather than derive the range with "because."

Also, "same output in four days" is misleading. Staff in the strongest study worked about 33–35 hours, including overtime, so not four standard days. A fairer phrase is "near-same output with about 12% fewer hours worked."

## Caveats dropped

**6. The mediation result (point 4 and the bottom line).** Source 5's own Limitations section notes that mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding. In addition:
- The test uses the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis.
- It covers one public employer.

The briefing should present it as "in one trial, about half the gain was associated with fewer meetings" and keep it out of the general bottom line.

*From my earlier critique, not in the sources:*
- With 14 clusters, the narrow interval needs checking.
- The log-hours denominator likely excludes meetings, which changes what a "meetings effect" would mean.

**7. Sickness and resignations (point 5).** "Real benefits… in every source" overstates them.
- **Halden's 36%:** visible in source 1 alone, a four-day schedule mechanically removes about 20% of the days on which anyone can be sick. That needs addressing before calling the fall real.
- **Varden's rota:** the arrangement was never stated, so the same may apply.
- **Resignations:** Varden's estimate is imprecise by its authors' own account; Halden's is uncontrolled and measured during the pilot itself.
- **Reporting:** the meta-analysis's "fell in all 14 that reported it" invites the question of which studies didn't report.

"Substantial falls in recorded sick days, partly arithmetic; lower resignations, imprecisely estimated" is closer to the evidence.

**8. Coverage-bound "per-hour gains" (point 3).** Higher output per hour with fewer staff present during unchanged opening hours is largely higher utilisation: staff have less idle time because the public waits longer. *(This is my earlier point; the sources call it a gain.)* Separately, "requires about 12% more staff" is one county's estimate. It should be attributed, along with its estimated +9% cost per contact.

**9. The binary classification.** Source 5 reports that a marketing agency, deadline-driven and so *discretionary* under source 4's coding, reverted over client deadlines. Calling coverage-bound work "the most consistent finding" is fair. But the briefing should note that the discretionary/coverage split is a simplification, as source 4 itself says.

## Omissions that matter for a policy group

**10. Cost.** None of the sources reports cost per unit of output, and the briefing doesn't flag this.
- Treated offices claimed overtime (timesheet hours fell only 12–13%).
- Pay stayed at full rate.
- Output per worker fell 2–4%.

Together, these mean cost per case almost certainly rose. A working group deciding on policy will ask this first. It belongs in §4.

**11. Backlog and time-to-decision.** These were never reported, even though source 2 raised statutory deadlines as a risk. A steady case-closure rate can hide a growing backlog. This also belongs among the open questions.

**12. Contamination in the control arm.** Two Varden control offices cut meetings at month 15. That raised control output and would shrink the measured treatment effect. So part of the "decline" may be control offices improving, not the treatment fading. *(My point, but visible from source 5's own data.)* This should be added to the open question on decline.

## What's done well

- **Section 4** identifies the most important open question: whether the cut in hours is needed, or whether reorganisation alone would deliver the gain. It also notes the evidence's limits beyond two years and outside the public sector.
- **The handling of source 3** is fair: its measurement findings stand, and its overreach is rejected.
- **The overall shape of the answer** is correct: a conditional answer, moderate per-hour gains, roughly maintained output per worker in discretionary work, and clear losses in coverage-bound work.

## A tighter bottom line

> In discretionary work, mostly evidenced in public administration, a 20% cut in scheduled hours reduced actual hours by 11–14% and raised output per actual hour by roughly 8–10%. Output per worker was 2–4% lower, with intervals including zero. The gain may have declined between 9 and 24 months, though this isn't statistically established. In one trial, about half of it was associated with fewer meetings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at higher cost. Cost per unit of output, backlog effects, durability beyond two years, and whether reorganisation without an hours cut would achieve similar gains remain open.

That is less tidy, but every clause in it is something the five sources support.

If useful, I can produce a revised version of the full briefing with these changes, keeping its structure.
